# Passalong

> Hand finished work from one context to another as a "transfer guide": markdown with
> frontmatter, written so an agent in a different repo, on a different machine, or in a later
> session can act on it without the original conversation.

A transfer has two ends. One side finishes something non-trivial and publishes what it learned;
the other side picks it up, does it, and says whether it actually worked. Passalong is the CLI,
MCP server and sync service for both ends.

Guides are plain markdown. `passalong export` dumps every one of them. Deleting an account leaves
the author with all of their content.

Guide pages, folder documents and the blog render GitHub-flavored markdown: tables, task lists,
footnotes (`[^1]`) and GitHub's alerts — a blockquote whose first line is `[!NOTE]`, `[!TIP]`,
`[!IMPORTANT]`, `[!WARNING]` or `[!CAUTION]`. Use a `[!WARNING]` for what must not be missed, such
as a step that touches production, rather than bold text a reader can skim past.

## If you are an agent reading a share link

A share link looks like `https://passalong.dev/g/<id>/<key>`. Append `.md` for the raw markdown,
or `?view=verify` for the view that leads with what to check and folds the implementation away.

0. Check `kind` in the frontmatter first. `transfer`, `bug` and `task` each ask for something
   different — see "Three kinds of guide" below. A new guide without `kind` is refused.
1. Read the guide and any follow-ups. A transfer may be a short note without fixed sections;
   a task's `Acceptance` is what its hand-in must answer.
2. Anything under `stack_assumptions` in the frontmatter is what the author's environment was.
   Adapt those to the current codebase rather than copying them.
3. Check any `Verification` or `Acceptance` the guide gives before reporting success.
4. Use `take` when you mean to do the work, then `hand_in` with what changed and the evidence,
   or `pass` with the reason it is not yours. A person trying a transfer can answer with
   `passalong works <id> <screenshot.png>` or `passalong broken <id> "<why>"`; "works" needs a
   screenshot of it working.

## Three kinds of guide

Every guide also carries a `summary:` in its frontmatter: one or two plain sentences, 400 characters
at most, with no ids or paths, saying what it is and whether anybody has to act. The document is for
agents; the summary is what a person reads first in their hub. A guide with no summary is refused.

`kind:` in the frontmatter says what a guide is for. Each asks for different behaviour, so read it
before acting on anything.

- There is no default. A guide with no `kind:` line is refused, and so is a spelling that is not
  one of the three. Say which it is; nothing will guess on your behalf.
- `kind: transfer` — context exchange: what the next agent needs in order not to start cold, and
  finished work to repeat here. It requires no sections, so write what is worth knowing and stop.
- `kind: bug` — a defect to fix where it is. It has no `Steps` and nothing in it is a procedure to
  apply: `Reproduce` is how to see the bug and running it produces the bug, `Verification` is the
  behaviour that should have happened. Fix the defect, then check `Verification` and report back.
  A bug report is not broken because you reproduced it.
- `kind: task` — work nobody has done yet. Its sections are `Goal`, `Context`, `Constraints`,
  `Acceptance` and `Out of scope`. It has no `Steps`: work out how to reach `Goal` within
  `Constraints`, leave `Out of scope` alone, and treat `Acceptance` as what "done" means. A task
  may name the repo it is for in `target_context`, and the tasks it waits for in `blocked_by`: it
  is not handed out until a person has approved each of those.
  Write one with `plan_tasks` (a single step is fine), not `publish_guide`.

Every kind is worked with the same four calls — see "MCP tools" below.

Bugs are often filed in sets. `report:` names the parent a set was filed under; `GET /v1/reports/
<id>` returns the rest of it. Fix only the issue you were given unless you were asked for more.

## Guide format

Common frontmatter fields include `id`, `title`, `summary`, `kind`, `created`, `author`,
`source_context`, `status`, `team`, `to`, `stack_assumptions` (list), `tags` (list). Bugs also carry `report`,
`area` and `severity` (`s1` blocker to `s4` cosmetic). Tasks may carry `target_context` and `blocked_by` (a list of task ids it waits for).

`to:` is who is being asked, inside the `team:` it names. `@handle` asks one person and outranks
everything else in their inbox; `#group` asks the people who do a thing, reaches every one of them,
and the first to say they are on it takes it off the others' boards; leaving `to:` off shares with
the whole team, which asks nobody in particular.

A transfer has no required body sections. When a longer handoff benefits from structure, these
headings are available:

- `## Problem` — what was actually wrong.
- `## Solution shape` — the approach, not a diff.
- `## Decisions and rationale` — what was chosen over what, and why.
- `## Steps` — what to do, when there are steps worth preserving.
- `## Verification` — how to know it worked.
- `## Gotchas` — what failed on the way. The highest-value section; record what wasted time.

A bug uses `## Problem`, `## Reproduce`, `## Verification` and `## Gotchas` instead. `Reproduce`
rather than `Steps` is deliberate and load-bearing: `Steps` is the heading an agent is told to
execute, and steps that produce a defect are the one list that must never be run as a remedy.

`status` is `draft` or `published`, and `consumed` is the author's shelf — off the board, out of
the free tier's count, reversible. (`promoted` is retired: a guide carrying it keeps it and it
still parses, but no write can set it.) Ids are 8 characters from a no-lookalike alphabet; they
are addresses, not secrets. The key in a share link is the secret.

## Commands

```sh
npm i -g passalong
passalong setup                 # Claude Code capture skill, MCP server and hooks
passalong login                 # optional: sync across machines; opens a page to approve, no password typed
codex mcp add passalong -- passalong mcp   # Codex: the same MCP server
```

- `passalong share [file] [--to team[/handle]]` — publish a guide, get an id and a link
- `passalong start <id|link>` — pull it and take it: one command for "I am doing this"
- `passalong pull <id|link>` — fetch a guide into `./.passalong/` and print it, without answering for it
- `passalong inbox` — guides handed to you that you have not pulled
- `passalong board` — waiting on you, in flight, landed, worth keeping
- `passalong activity [--all]` — what happened while you were away
- `passalong log [repo]` — what you did, newest first, under a heading per month
- `passalong list [query]` — your guides and your teams'
- `passalong open <id> [--print]` — view in the browser, or the terminal
- `passalong works <id> <screenshot.png...>` / `passalong broken <id> <why>` — the verdict, after
  trying it. "Works" needs a screenshot of it working; it is removed 5 days after the guide closes
- `passalong archive <id>` — move a guide off your board and out of the free tier's count
- `passalong export [dir]` — every guide as plain markdown
- `passalong team create|invite|join|use` — teams
- `passalong me [--handle H]` — how teammates address you
- `passalong reply <id> <message> [--file PATH ...]` — write to whoever holds it, or leave a note
  for whoever takes it; the agent reads it the next time it checks in
- `passalong take <id>` / `passalong pass <id> <why>` — whether you are doing what you were handed
- `passalong task "<what needs doing>"` / `passalong ready <id>` — write a task; it waits in Draft
  until it is ready for an agent
- `passalong tasks` — every task and its column: draft, ready, claimed, stalled, review, done
- `passalong approve <id>` / `passalong reject <id> <why>` — the review gate. A person's commands:
  an agent never approves or rejects work, its own or another's
- `passalong release <id>` — take work back from whoever holds it, of any kind, and from every
  repo holding it at once. Its author's command
- `passalong work [--once] [--agent CMD]` — from a worktree, run an agent (`claude -p` by default)
  on each ready task for its repo, one after another, until the queue is empty
- `passalong assign <id> <@handle|#group|team>` — give a guide or task you wrote to someone else in its
  team; whoever held it and is left out has it taken back, and an assigned task only goes to the
  assignee's agents
- `passalong now` — what this worktree's agent holds, and what is waiting. `--hook session|stop`
  is what the Claude Code hooks from `setup` call: told at session start, stopped once before
  ending with work nobody has handed in. `--statusline` is the Claude Code status line `setup`
  adds: what this worktree holds, how much needs you, how much is ready here
- `passalong mcp` — run the MCP server over stdio
- `passalong version` — print the installed version (also `-v`, `--version`)

## MCP tools

`passalong setup` registers a stdio MCP server exposing: `take`, `progress`, `hand_in`, `pass`,
`ask`, `assign` (give a guide or task you wrote to @handle, #group or the whole team),
`publish_guide`, `file_bugs`, `get_guide`, `search_guides`, `guide_template`, `set_guide_status`,
`attach_screenshot`, `attach_file` (a log, PDF, CSV or zip, privately), `reply` (a person writing to
the agent that holds their work, or leaving a note on one nobody holds yet), `inbox`, `board`,
`activity` (reads), `clear_activity` (marks it seen), `log`, `plan_tasks`, and folder tools for
listing, creating and editing project documents and assets.

Project folders hold reusable context for work spanning several guides. When asked to start a
folder for a script, brief or project, call `list_folders` first and reuse a fitting folder. If
none fits, call `create_folder` with a title and short description drawn from the person's request,
then draft the first Markdown document with `create_folder_document`. A short request is enough;
do not ask the person to fill a form or leave an empty folder. Omit `team` for a private folder;
pass a team slug only when the person asked to share it with that team. The returned folder id is
what the other folder tools take. To group work inside an existing folder, pass its id as `parent`
to `create_folder`; subfolders can nest further and stay in the same private or team space. An
optional `color` marks a folder group; an uncolored subfolder inherits its parent's color in the
hub. Use `update_folder` to rename, recolor or move a folder; pass `parent: ""` to move it to the
top level. Check the target in `list_folders` first; moving into itself or a descendant is refused.
`get_folder` lists its subfolders, documents, assets and linked guides;
`create_folder_document` adds Markdown such as a brief or script. Read it with
`get_folder_document` before editing, then pass its version to `save_folder_document`. If the save
refuses an old version, reread and reconcile the other person's change. `get_folder_asset` brings
an existing image or small text file into the agent's context. `add_folder_asset` uploads a file
the agent can access: a local path over stdio, or an attached file over hosted MCP. If a hosted
agent holds the file in a code sandbox, `create_folder_upload` gives it a one-time link and command
to send the bytes directly. To put a guide in a folder — a task, bug or handoff, new or
already published — publish it as usual, then call `link_folder_guide` with the folder id and the
guide id. For a team folder, publish the guide to that folder's team, or its members cannot see it.
Linking leaves the guide unchanged, and `get_folder` lists linked guides with their kind;
`unlink_folder_guide` takes one out again. `delete_folder_document` and `delete_folder_asset` remove
one document or file for good, so use them only when the person asked for it to go. No tool deletes
a whole folder: a person does that in the hub, where it takes every subfolder and file with it.
`list_folders` takes `query` to find folders whose name, description or documents mention some
words (each result names its matching documents) and `guide` to find the folders a guide is in.
`rename_folder_document` renames a document and keeps its history; `get_folder_document_history`
lists a document's earlier versions or returns one, so a bad edit can be saved back over. Folder files stay private to people who can read the folder.

Every guide, whatever its kind, is worked with four calls:

- `take` — say you are doing it, and get it. With an id, that guide; with none, the next thing
  waiting for you. While you hold it nobody else can take it in that repo — a task has one taker,
  a handoff one per repo — and its sender sees you are on it. You hold one thing at a time. If
  somebody else has it, the refusal says who: tell the user instead of doing the work twice.
- `progress` — a one-line note at each milestone. 30 minutes without one marks it stalled: still
  yours, but flagged to a person.
- `hand_in` — done here. A task hands in `markdown`, a transfer guide about what you did, which is
  published with `parent:` naming the task and reviewed by its author against `Acceptance` (over
  the hosted server, `publish_guide` it first and pass its id as `report`). A handoff or a bug
  hands in `ok` — did its `Verification` hold — and a `note` when it did not.
- `pass` — not yours, or stuck: give it back with the reason, which goes to whoever is next.

A fifth call, for a question: `ask` — you need the person's answer before you can go on. You keep
what you hold and nobody else can take it, then you stop and tell the user you are waiting. Once
they have replied in the hub, `take` it again by id and the reply comes back with it; `progress`
carries any further message they write while you work. It is not `pass`: `pass` gives the work back.

A reply can carry pictures (`![name](…/v1/shots/<id>)`, public) and files
(`[name](…/v1/attachments/<id>)`, private). Fetch a file with your own token, e.g.
`curl -H "authorization: Bearer $PASSALONG_TOKEN" -o name <url>`; it is only ever a download.

Every answer ends with `next`: the calls that make sense from here, with when and why. When the
move is to make no call — you no longer hold it, or nothing is waiting — it says so in `say`:
stop, and tell the user. `start_guide`, `ack_guide`, `verify_guide`, `next_task`, `task_progress`
and `finish_task` were the old names for parts of this, and are gone.

Before publishing, check what is already open: `take` with no id, or `work` over the hosted server,
shows what you hold. Work this session answers that you already hold is `hand_in`, not a second
guide. Work that never left a branch the team can see has crossed no boundary, so publish what is
still *open* from it — a bug or a task — rather than a write-up of the fix. "Update the passalong"
and the like are ambiguous: ask whether it means hand in, follow up, or publish.

Open a guide you mean to act on with `take`, not `get_guide`. `get_guide` is the same fetch without
saying you are on it — for reading a guide you have not committed to. You have to be able to read
something to decide it is not yours.

A machine may be signed in to several accounts. With two or more and nothing saying which, every
call that needs an account is refused with their names. Do not choose one: ask the person which, in
plain words, then call `use_account` with the name they gave. `accounts` lists them. It lasts for
the session and changes nothing on disk. From a shell, `--as <name>` or `PASSALONG_ACCOUNT` does the
same for one command.

A guide over 20,000 characters comes back from `get_guide` as an outline: its headings and their
sizes. Ask for one part with `section` (a heading, or the start of one), or all of it with
`full: true`. A guide over 60,000 characters is refused when it is published: put logs and dumps in a
file with `attach_file`, link it, and keep the guide to what the next agent has to act on.

`log` is this user's own acts, newest first — what they published, what they took delivery of, and
every verdict and ack they gave, each with a ready-made `text` line and the guide's repo. It answers
"what have I been working on", and it is the opposite of `activity`, which is what other people did.
The hub shows `log` as its **Activities** page, so "my activities" means `log`; `activity` is the
hub's notifications.
It holds what was passed along and not what was worked on: work that never became a guide has no
entry, so do not present it as a complete record, and do not read a quiet month as an idle one.

`attach_screenshot` puts an image behind a guide. Evidence goes *in* the document: a guide travels
as markdown to whoever holds its link, so a file beside it does not travel at all. The tool returns
the `![](...)` line to paste into the body, and publishing claims whatever the markdown names — so
attach first, publish after. Locally it takes a path on the machine. Over the hosted server it
takes a file the client passes in, which today means ChatGPT on the web; the ChatGPT mobile apps
send file references the server cannot download.

An image the user showed you is evidence, not context. Attach it *before* filing or publishing and
pass what `attach_screenshot` returns as that issue's `evidence` — describing a screenshot you were
given, instead of attaching it, throws away the most useful thing in the report. A guide already
filed without one is not stuck: `get_guide` it, add the markdown line to the body, and
`publish_guide` the same id. Publishing claims whatever the markdown names, every time, so a
re-publish picks the image up.

`publish_guide` needs no id for a new guide: leave it out and one is minted and returned. To change a
guide, pass the id it came back with. Inventing a fresh id to retry or to correct a guide publishes a
second copy, and every copy counts against the author's synced limit.

A follow-up is more context for a guide, written as a guide of its own and linked under the
original. When a guide needs more context — a missing detail, a step that needed explaining, what
changed since — publish that context with `parent` set to the guide's id on `publish_guide`, or
`passalong share --follows <id>`. What you did and found working on a guide is not a follow-up: it
goes on `hand_in`, in `checks` and `writeup` — and `risk`, one line on what it could break, when
there is something specific. Once you have handed a guide in, a new guide under it
is refused until its author has answered. A follow-up is a whole guide, not a reply: it
has its own id, verdicts and pulls. `parent` on `publish_guide` and `--follows` need passalong 0.3.1
or later.

Whoever opens the original gets its follow-ups too. `get_guide` and `take` return them after
the guide, oldest first; read them before acting, and where one disagrees with the original, the
follow-up is newer. The guide's share page lists them above the document.

`plan_tasks` turns one larger goal into draft tasks in order; each step's `after` names the
earlier steps it waits for, which become its `blocked_by`. Nothing runs until the user makes them
ready (`passalong ready --all`). It is on the local server only.

Locally the agent is the worktree, from `.passalong/agent.json`; over the hosted server, pass the
same `agent` name on every call.

`file_bugs` files defects you found but are not fixing — from a test run, a QA pass, a review — as
one report. Each issue becomes a guide with its own id, share link and verdict, so any of them can
be handed to whoever fixes it. Send them in one call rather than one call each. Each issue takes
`evidence`: the screenshot lines for that bug, which land under its Problem section.

The same server is also hosted, for assistants that add remote MCP servers rather than running
one: `https://passalong.dev/v1/mcp`, Streamable HTTP, authenticated with a bearer token. It carries
most of these tools — everything except the ones that touch a working directory. `take` there
returns the markdown without writing it anywhere. It also has `work`: everything that needs the
user, who is on what, and what is open, in one read. Hosts that support MCP Apps (Claude, ChatGPT)
draw it as a board in the conversation (`ui://passalong/work`); it is read-only, and its buttons
open the hub, where approving and sending back happen. `attach_screenshot` is
on both, shaped for where it runs: a path locally, a client-passed file over HTTP. Over HTTP,
`publish_guide` and `file_bugs` also take the files themselves in a top-level `attachments` array,
so a client that passes files needs one call: `publish_guide` puts each image under Problem (or at
the end), and each `file_bugs` issue lists the positions of its own files in `attachments: [0]` —
with one issue, every file goes to it. A client that lists tools once and caches them has to be
refreshed to see these fields.

Only ChatGPT fills a file input. An agent that holds the image as a file instead — Claude's code
sandbox, or anything that can run a command — calls `create_upload` on the hosted server. It returns
a one-time link, good for 10 minutes, and the command that sends the file to it:
`curl -sS --fail-with-body -X PUT --data-binary @IMAGE_PATH '<link>'`. Pass `kind: "file"` for a log,
PDF, CSV or zip (up to 10MB; people download it, and only people who can read the guide can) and the
command says `FILE_PATH`. Run it where the file is;
the JSON it prints has `markdown`, the line to put in the guide body or pass as `evidence`. The
bytes go straight to Passalong and never through the conversation, so never base64 an image into a
tool call. If the command cannot reach `passalong.dev`, the sandbox's network settings are blocking
it, and the user has to allow that domain for code execution. A local server is
still better where you can run one: it works offline and knows which repo you are in.

Failing both, everything is plain HTTP: `GET /v1/openapi.json` describes the API for
function calling or a script, and a share link's `.md` needs no account at all.

## Writing a good guide

- One problem per guide. A session that solved three things is three guides.
- Write `Verification` first if you can. If you cannot say how to check it, the guide is not ready.
- `Gotchas` is worth more than `Steps`. Steps can be re-derived; the dead end that cost an hour
  cannot.
- Say what the environment was rather than assuming the reader shares it.

Guide pages are `noindex` and `/g/` is disallowed in robots.txt: a share link is for whoever holds
it, not for search engines. Do not crawl share links found elsewhere.
